title: Around the mountain
hook: the pilgrimage around Mount Kailash, sacred to several traditions

segments.voice: Yesterday, eighty-eight temples: pilgrims in white circling Kukai's island, an orange held out on a country road. Your line was eighty-eight temples. What kindness did you receive with a bow? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

Snow on a black pyramid of rock, alone above a high, bare plateau in western Tibet. Pilgrims don't walk up it. They walk around it. A family walks together, the youngest riding on a father's shoulders. A young man lies flat on the stony path, stretches his arms forward, marks the spot, stands, steps to the mark, and lies down again, measuring the whole circle with his body. A group of pilgrims from India moves past, chanting a different name for the same mountain. And now and then, someone comes the other way, walking the circle in the opposite direction. The mountain is Kailash. Today's word is what they're all doing: around the mountain.
screen: `SNOW ON A BLACK PEAK.` → `PILGRIMS DON'T CLIMB IT.` → `THEY WALK AROUND IT.`

segments.voice: First, a very old gesture. Walking around something holy, keeping it on your right, is a way Buddhists show respect, and it goes back to the texts. In the old discourses, again and again, someone who has listened to the Buddha rises, bows, and departs keeping him on the right. So circling a stupa, a temple or a mountain clockwise carries that same bow forward, step by step. Second, the mountain. For Tibetan Buddhists, Kailash is the home of a great meditation deity, and the circle around it, called a kora, is a pilgrimage they hold dear. The path climbs to a high pass, where pilgrims hang prayer flags and some leave behind a small thing of their own, a bit of cloth, a lock of hair, as a sign of leaving the old life on the mountain. Third, the neighbors. Kailash is not only a Buddhist mountain. Hindus honor it as the dwelling of Shiva. Jains revere it as a place of liberation. Followers of Bon, the old religion of Tibet, hold it sacred too, and they walk the circle counterclockwise, by their own custom. So on the same path, people of several faiths pass one another, going around the same peak, each for their own reasons, and nobody has to agree to share the trail. Fourth, why around and not up. Tradition holds the summit is not to be climbed. The center stays untouched. The pilgrimage is the circle.
screen: `KEEPING IT ON THE RIGHT.` · `THE KORA AND THE HIGH PASS.` · `SEVERAL FAITHS, ONE TRAIL.` · then, large: `THE CENTER STAYS UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: Here is a way to walk a kora at home, if you'd like. Choose a center: a plant, a candle, a chair, an image that means something to you. Walk slowly around it clockwise, keeping it on your right. Feel your feet, and your shoulder turned toward the center. Go around a few times, or just once, slowly. If you can't walk, trace the circle with your eyes. Then stop facing the center, and stand or sit with it for a moment. You don't need to reach it. You're circling it. The bell holds the time.
Around the mountain. The kora around Mount Kailash, walked by Buddhists and by people of several other faiths, circling a peak that tradition says is not to be climbed. Today's word.

Your line: around the mountain. Today, when you pass something that matters to you, a photo, a tree, a place of worship, keep it on your right for a few steps. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist pilgrims walk the kora around Mount Kailash clockwise, some making full-body prostrations along the way, and Buddhists also circle stupas and temples clockwise as a sign of respect.

notes: Recurring Nikaya formula: a visitor rises, pays homage and departs 'keeping him on the right' (padakkhinam katva). Cited to DN 2's close as an example; confirm the reference.
Kailash for Tibetan Buddhists as the abode of Chakrasamvara (Demchok), described here as 'a great meditation deity'; confirm.
Neighbors described briefly and without ranking: Hindus (Shiva's dwelling), Jains (a place of liberation, associated with Rishabhanatha), Bon (counterclockwise). Confirm each is fair.
Dolma La pass customs (prayer flags, leaving cloth or hair) are given as what 'some' do; confirm.
'Tradition holds the summit is not to be climbed': confirm phrasing.
